title: Why does rubbing a bump help?

scenes.heading: Why does *rubbing it* help?
scenes.narration: You bump your elbow and, without thinking, you rub it. And it actually helps a little. Why?

scenes.title: Wait, or rub?
scenes.narration: If you just wait, the pain signal travels up your spinal cord at full volume. If you rub it, a second signal joins in: touch, on thick, fast fibers.

scenes.title: The gate
scenes.narration: In your spinal cord, touch switches on small neurons that act like a gate, turning down the pain signal on its way up. That's an analogy: no real door, just neurons quieting neurons.

scenes.title: Only a dimmer
scenes.narration: Scientists call this the gate control theory. It's simplified, but touch really can dim pain. And your brain can turn the gate down too.

scenes.title: Remember
scenes.narration: So rubbing doesn't fix the bump, it turns the volume down. What do you do when you bump your elbow? The full video is on the channel.
scenes.cta: What do you do? Tell me ▶

notes: Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965): large touch fibers (Aβ) excite inhibitory neurons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, which reduce the pain signal going up. Influential, now considered oversimplified (Wikipedia, "Gate control theory"; University of Iowa pressbook, "Pain": pressure near an injury decreases pain through inhibitory interneurons).
Descending control: pathways from the brainstem can inhibit pain signals in the spinal cord (MSU open textbook, "Pain").
Rubbing only dims the pain; it does not treat the injury. The example is a bumped elbow, never a burn.
Simplified drawing: one fiber of each kind, one relay neuron. Real nerves carry thousands of fibers.
Educational only, no first aid or treatment advice. If a pain or an injury worries you, see a professional.
